q: Phenylacetonitrile is heated at reflux in aqueous H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> for several hours. What is the organic product?
h: Full hydrolysis of a nitrile goes through an amide. Where does it end?
w: Water adds to the protonated C≡N to give an amide, which under prolonged heating in acid is hydrolyzed further (NH4+ released). The nitrile carbon becomes the CO2H carbon, so no carbon is lost: A, phenylacetic acid.
x: The amide is the intermediate; several hours at reflux in strong acid hydrolyze it on to the carboxylic acid.
An amine would require a reducing agent such as LiAlH<sub>4</sub>; aqueous acid only hydrolyzes.
The nitrile carbon is kept as the carboxyl carbon; benzoic acid has one carbon too few.

h: The product has one more carbon than the starting halide. Which group adds a carbon that can become CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>?
w: SN2 with cyanide gives butanenitrile (one new carbon). LiAlH4 adds two hydrides to C≡N, and workup gives the primary amine with the nitrile carbon as CH2: 1. NaCN 2. LiAlH4 3. H2O.
x: Ammonia substitution gives propan-1-amine (three carbons), and over-alkylation gives di- and tripropylamines.
Acid hydrolysis of the nitrile gives butanoic acid, not the amine.
A Grignard adds to the nitrile and, after hydrolysis, gives a ketone (pentan-2-one).

q: What is the product after aqueous acid workup?
h: The Grignard adds once to C≡N. What does the resulting C=N species become in aqueous acid?
w: EtMgBr adds to the nitrile carbon to give an imine magnesium salt (C=N–MgBr). Aqueous acid protonates it to the imine, which hydrolyzes to the ketone: A, 1-phenylpropan-1-one (propiophenone).
x: Two additions do not occur: the negatively charged imine salt is not electrophilic enough to react with a second Grignard.
No hydride source is present to reduce C=N to an amine.
The imine is an intermediate; aqueous acid hydrolyzes it to the ketone.

q: An ester and excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr give a 3° alcohol, but a nitrile and excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr give a ketone after workup. What is the best explanation?
c: The nitrile adduct is an anionic imine salt that cannot react with a second Grignard; the ketone forms only during workup
Nitriles are more reactive than ketones, so the Grignard is used up before the ketone forms
The ketone formed from the nitrile is protected because it is immediately deprotonated to an enolate
Nitrogen is a better leaving group than oxygen, so the C=N bond is never formed
h: Follow the nitrile reaction step by step. When does the ketone C=O actually appear?
w: With an ester, the tetrahedral intermediate expels the alkoxide in the flask, so a ketone forms in the presence of Grignard and is attacked again. With a nitrile, addition gives R2C=N− MgBr+. There is no leaving group, and the negatively charged imine salt is not electrophilic, so it waits. The ketone appears only when aqueous acid hydrolyzes the imine, after the Grignard has been destroyed.
x: Nitriles are actually less electrophilic than ketones; the explanation is that no ketone is present until workup.
No ketone exists in the flask before workup, so enolization is not what protects it.
Nothing leaves from the nitrile adduct; that is exactly why it stops at the imine salt. Amide ions are also very poor leaving groups.

h: DIBAL-H delivers one hydride to C≡N. What does the resulting imine-aluminum species become in water?
w: One hydride adds to the nitrile carbon, giving an aluminum-bound imine (C=N–Al). It cannot accept a second hydride easily, and aqueous workup hydrolyzes the imine to A, 3-methylbutanal.
x: Two hydrides (from LiAlH<sub>4</sub>) give the primary amine; DIBAL-H stops after one.
DIBAL-H reduces; it does not hydrolyze the nitrile to an acid.
The nitrogen is lost as NH<sub>3</sub> during hydrolysis of the imine; the carbon ends as CHO, not CH<sub>2</sub>OH.

q: Which sequence best converts 2-bromo-2-methylpropane into 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCO<sub>2</sub>H?
h: Both the nitrile route and the Grignard/CO<sub>2</sub> route add one carbon. Which one needs an S<sub>N</sub>2 step?
w: Making a tertiary Grignard is fine (no SN2 needed); it adds to CO2 to give a carboxylate, and acid gives the acid: 1. Mg 2. CO2 3. H3O+. The cyanide route needs SN2 at a tertiary carbon, which fails; cyanide acts as a base and gives 2-methylpropene by E2.
x: Cyanide cannot do S<sub>N</sub>2 at a tertiary carbon; elimination to 2-methylpropene dominates, so little nitrile forms.
At best this route forms tert-butyl alcohol (with much 2-methylpropene), which has no H on the carbinol carbon and cannot be oxidized; it also never adds the needed extra carbon.
Besides the failed S<sub>N</sub>2 step, LiAlH<sub>4</sub> would reduce a nitrile to an amine, not a carboxylic acid.

q: What is the final organic product?
h: Two things happen in hot aqueous acid: both esters are hydrolyzed, and then one structural feature of the diacid makes it unstable to heat.
w: Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes both ethyl esters to give benzylmalonic acid. A malonic acid has a C=O β to the other CO2H, so on heating it loses CO2 through a cyclic six-membered transition state, giving an enol of a carboxylic acid that tautomerizes: A, 3-phenylpropanoic acid.
x: Benzylmalonic acid forms first, but a 1,3-diacid decarboxylates on heating; it does not survive the conditions.
Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the ester, so the ethyl ester does not remain.
Only one CO<sub>2</sub> is lost; after the first decarboxylation there is no longer a β-carbonyl to allow a second one. Phenylacetic acid has one carbon too few.

q: Which acid loses CO<sub>2</sub> readily when warmed to about 100 °C?
h: Easy thermal decarboxylation needs a C=O two carbons away from the carboxyl carbon, so that a six-membered cyclic transition state can form.
w: A β-keto acid has the ketone C=O β to the CO2H. The carboxyl H is transferred to the ketone oxygen through a six-membered cyclic transition state while the C–C bond breaks, giving CO2 and an enol. A, 3-oxobutanoic acid (acetoacetic acid), is the β-keto acid; it decarboxylates to acetone.
x: Pyruvic acid is an α-keto acid; the C=O is too close to form the six-membered cyclic transition state.
4-Oxopentanoic acid is a γ-keto acid; the ketone is too far away for the cyclic transition state, and the C–C bond breaking would not give a stabilized enol.
Benzoic acid has no β-carbonyl; aryl carboxylic acids need much harsher conditions to lose CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: 3-Oxobutanoic acid loses CO2 on heating through a cyclic transition state. What is the first-formed organic product (before any tautomerization)?
h: In the cyclic transition state the carboxyl H moves to the ketone oxygen while the C–CO<sub>2</sub> bond breaks. Where do those C–C bonding electrons go?
w: Six electrons move around a ring: the ketone oxygen takes the carboxyl H, the O–H bond electrons become the second C=O of CO2, and the breaking C–C bond electrons form a C=C between the α-carbon and the former ketone carbon. No charged intermediate forms; the first product is the neutral enol, A (prop-1-en-2-ol), which then tautomerizes to acetone.
x: Acetone is the final product, formed by keto–enol tautomerization of the enol; it is not the first-formed species.
The concerted cyclic pathway is neutral throughout; no carbanion is produced (that would be very unstable without a counter-ion).
Methylketene would require losing water, not CO<sub>2</sub>, and has the wrong connectivity.

q: A carboxylic acid derivative has the IR spectrum shown (two strong C=O bands at 1820 and 1760 cm<sup>−1</sup>; no O–H or N–H bands). Which compound is it?
h: Which derivative has two C=O groups that can stretch in phase and out of phase?
w: An anhydride has two coupled C=O groups, giving a symmetric and an asymmetric stretch, typically near 1820 and 1760 cm−1. The pair of strong high-frequency bands identifies A, propanoic anhydride.
x: An acid chloride shows one C=O band near 1800 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not a pair.
An ester shows a single C=O near 1735–1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
A carboxylic acid would show a very broad O–H band from about 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=O near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Rank the compounds by C=O stretching frequency, lowest to highest wavenumber.
h: Resonance donation into C=O lengthens and weakens it (lower wavenumber); inductive withdrawal shortens and strengthens it.
w: In the amide (III) the N lone pair donates strongly, giving the C=O much single-bond character: ~1650 cm−1. In the ester (I) oxygen donates less and withdraws inductively: ~1740 cm−1. In the acid chloride (II) Cl hardly donates and withdraws strongly: ~1800 cm−1. Order: III < I < II.
x: This reverses the order. More resonance donation means a weaker C=O and a lower wavenumber, so the amide is lowest.
The ester's oxygen donates less than the amide nitrogen, so the ester C=O is at higher wavenumber than the amide.
Chlorine is the poorest π donor and withdraws inductively, so the acid chloride has the highest C=O stretch, not the ester.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows strong IR bands at 1742 and 1240 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no band above 3100 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown. What is the compound?
h: The IR says ester. Then look at where the CH<sub>2</sub> quartet is: on oxygen (~4 ppm) or next to C=O (~2.3 ppm)?
w: 1742 and 1240 cm−1 (C=O and C–O) with no O–H band mean an ester. A 3H singlet at 2.05 ppm is a CH3 on C=O. The 2H quartet at 4.12 ppm is an OCH2 next to a CH3 (triplet at 1.26). So the ethyl is on oxygen and the methyl is on the carbonyl: A, ethyl acetate.
x: Methyl propanoate would show an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near 3.7 ppm and a CH<sub>2</sub> quartet near 2.3 ppm (next to C=O), not 4.1 ppm.
Propyl formate would show a formyl H singlet near 8.0 ppm (1H) and an OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet, not a quartet.
Butanoic acid would show a very broad O–H band in the IR (2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>) and a CO<sub>2</sub>H proton near 11–12 ppm.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR spectrum shown: two medium bands at 3360 and 3180 cm<sup>−1</sup>, C–H at 2960 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and strong bands at 1660 and 1630 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which structure fits?
h: Two N–H stretches mean NH<sub>2</sub>. A C=O near 1660 cm<sup>−1</sup> is much lower than a ketone's.
w: Two N–H bands (symmetric and asymmetric stretch) show an NH2 group. A C=O at 1660 cm−1 (lowered by N donation) with an N–H bend near 1630 cm−1 is a primary amide: A, butanamide.
x: A secondary amide (N–H) shows only one N–H stretch, near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
A tertiary amide has no N–H bond, so it would show no bands at all above 3100 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
This amino ketone has NH<sub>2</sub> bands but a ketone C=O near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not 1660 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which sequence converts hexanoic acid into hexan-1-amine, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, with no change in the number of carbons?
h: Make an amide first. Then find the step that turns C=O into CH<sub>2</sub> while keeping the C–N bond.
w: SOCl2 gives hexanoyl chloride; excess NH3 gives hexanamide (the second equivalent takes up HCl). LiAlH4 reduces the amide C=O to CH2, keeping all six carbons: 1. SOCl2 2. NH3 3. LiAlH4 4. H2O.
x: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the acid to hexan-1-ol, and OH<sup>−</sup> is too poor a leaving group for ammonia to displace it.
Br<sub>2</sub>/NaOH on a primary amide is the Hofmann rearrangement, which loses the carbonyl carbon and gives pentan-1-amine.
Hot aqueous acid simply hydrolyzes the amide back to hexanoic acid.

q: Compound X, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>N, has a sharp IR band at 2250 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no bands above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>. X reacts with 1. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr 2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> to give 2-methylpentan-3-one. What is X?
h: Grignard + nitrile → ketone: the nitrile carbon becomes the C=O; the ethyl comes from the Grignard. What is on the other side of the C=O?
w: 2-Methylpentan-3-one is (CH3)2CH–CO–CH2CH3. The ethyl came from the Grignard, so the nitrile must be (CH3)2CH–C≡N. The 2250 cm−1 band (C≡N) and the formula C4H7N fit: A, 2-methylpropanenitrile.
x: Butanenitrile + EtMgBr gives hexan-3-one (unbranched), not 2-methylpentan-3-one.
An isocyanide (R–N≡C) absorbs near 2140 cm<sup>−1</sup> and does not give a ketone with a Grignard reagent.
A primary amine would show N–H stretches above 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and an internal alkyne C≡C is weak; it would not give a ketone with EtMgBr.
